message.content:
No, under the usual definition, such examples do not exist.
If X has a finite expectation, then its positive and negative parts have finite sums.
If Y also has a finite expectation, then its positive and negative parts have finite sums.
For the sum X plus Y, the positive part is bounded by the sum of positive parts.
The negative part is likewise bounded by the sum of negative parts.
Those bounds are finite when both individual expectations are finite.
Therefore the expectation of X plus Y is finite.
The linearity formula holds in this finite expectation setting.
Discreteness is not needed for this conclusion.
The statement is true for real valued random variables more generally.
The phrase undefined can arise with other sign configurations.
For example, one expectation may be positive infinity and another negative infinity.
In that case the sum expectation may be undefined.
But that situation does not have both individual expectations finite.
The reference text specifies finite expectations for X and Y.
That specification rules out the undefined sum case.
It also rules out an infinite sum expectation.
Finite individual means guarantee finite mean of the sum.
The key property is integrability.
Integrability means absolute expectation is finite.
If both variables are integrable, their sum is integrable.
Thus the answer to the reference question is no.
The standard answer to the reference text is no, because finite expectations for X and Y imply that X and Y are integrable, and integrable real valued random variables have an integrable sum beneath the standard rules of expectation.
